title: Topological Out-of-Domain Generalization in Dynamical Systems Reconstruction
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Prior models tie Jacobian scaling to fixed-point location through one shared feature; splitting features decouples them, as real systems require.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, blue vs orange boxes plus line plot
description: Panel A has two boxed diagrams side by side. The left, blue box shows the vanilla model. A single feature l fans out to weight vectors w_1 through w_K, which all feed both J(l) and x*(l). A double-headed arrow between those two outputs shows they are coupled. The right, orange box shows the proposed model. Feature l_d in red feeds the weights and J(l_d). Feature l_p in purple feeds x*(l_p, l_d). The double-headed arrow between the outputs is crossed out, meaning they are decoupled. Panel B is a line plot of the ratio ||J||_F/||x*|| against control parameter p for five textbook systems (Lorenz-63, Selkov, SIR, Van der Pol, FitzHugh-Nagumo). Their curves scale differently, from V-shaped to flat.
caption: Illustration of hierarchical DSR models. (A) Vanilla hierarchical model (left) uses a single feature vector $\bm{l}$ to obtain weights $\bm{w}_k$ of specific DSR model instantiations, which entangles the scaling of the Jacobian $\bm{J}(\bm{l})$ with the fixed point (FP) position $\bm{x}^*(\bm{l})$ as $\bm{l}$ changes. Conversely, utilizing independent features (right) $\bm{l}_d$ and $\bm{l}_p$ for the local dynamics and FP location enables the decoupled scaling observed in physical systems. (B) Examples of differential Jacobian-vs.-location scaling behavior with control parameter $p$ for different `textbook' examples of DS. $\|\cdot\|_F$ denotes the Frobenius norm; the Jacobian is evaluated at a constant point $\bm{x}_0$.
abstract: Predicting the behavior of dynamical systems (DS) beyond the dynamical and parameter regimes observed in training is a pivotal and essentially unresolved problem in scientific ML. It is central to any good scientific theory, which we expect to be able to make predictions about regimes not covered by currently available data. Recent hierarchical and hyper-network guided approaches for DS reconstruction (DSR) enable training on many DS simultaneously, and revealed that extracted latent features are often related to crucial control parameters of the underlying DS that varied across the training corpus. However, true out-of-domain forecasting abilities of these models, e.g., across tipping points, remain limited, and fine-tuning, or even full model retraining, on time series from the new dynamical regime is usually required. Here, we mathematically analyze the root of these limitations in previous model formulations and identify three core shortcomings rooted in a mismatch between structural assumptions of the reconstruction model and typical properties of physical systems. We propose a combination of remedies for these shortcomings, most importantly feature splitting, and furthermore derive a closed-form bound on the reliable extrapolation range. We demonstrate empirically that our techniques allow for accurate zero-shot prediction into new dynamical regimes, outside the observed training regime, as, e.g., encountered across tipping points.
